children: UPI MDR concerns raised by stockbrokers will be examined by SEBI ahead of the new 0.02% charge taking effect on October 15

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) will examine concerns raised by stockbrokers over the new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions, with the charge set to take effect from 15 October.

Sebi Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said the regulator would look into issues raised by the broking community over the impact of the new payment charge. The concerns centre on the possibility that brokers could incur a cost when clients transfer funds into their trading accounts but do not subsequently execute trades.

Under the new framework, UPI transactions linked to mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers, dealers and investment advisers will attract an MDR of 0.02 per cent, subject to a maximum charge of Rs 300 per transaction.

Brokers have argued that the MDR could create an additional operating cost because the charge is linked to the transfer of funds rather than the revenue generated from a subsequent trade. A client may transfer money to a brokerage account and leave it unused, meaning the broker could incur the UPI cost without earning brokerage revenue.
Brokers have also highlighted the impact of periodic settlement requirements, under which unused client funds are returned and may subsequently be transferred back through UPI.

New-age brokers including Groww, Zerodha, Upstox and Angel One are also preparing representations to Sebi on the proposed MDR structure. Their concerns include the Rs 300 cap and the threshold above which MDR applies.

Zerodha founder Nithin Kamath has separately argued that brokers may not be able to absorb the additional cost indefinitely because UPI transfers do not guarantee a corresponding trade or brokerage income.

The capital-market MDR is significantly lower than the 0.4 per cent rate applicable to eligible merchant transactions above Rs 2,000 under the broader UPI framework. Ordinary consumers are not expected to directly bear the MDR on these transactions.
Sebi’s review could determine whether the current structure needs changes for capital-market transactions, particularly where fund transfers do not result in actual investment or trading activity.
The regulator’s examination comes ahead of the implementation date, giving the industry and authorities time to assess the operational and cost implications for brokers.
